inserts.title: Matched simulations isolate the object's contribution
paragraphs: Conductivity describes how readily a material carries electric current, and an object's conductivity sets how strongly it distorts the field around it. Simulated scenes with and without the object were otherwise matched, so the difference between them reflects the object itself rather than other scene differences. The reconstruction keeps that difference as the signal of interest for each frame.

The pattern also depends on where the fish sits relative to the object. Each receptor samples a different part of the perturbation as the fish moves, so the same metal cube can generate different electric images at different positions. Each frame records the object's influence at every receptor location, and position is encoded alongside the object.

Because the reconstruction was built from real approaches, each image in the series corresponds to one moment in one fish's inspection. The estimates inherit the timing of the fish's own movement. Each reconstructed frame is a model output, not a snapshot taken by a camera. The frames follow the successive discharges emitted during the approach.
notes: Matched simulations isolate the object's contribution.

inserts.title: Image intensity and diameter both shift with distance
paragraphs: A rule based on image intensity fails here because intensity falls as an object moves away, while the rewarded physical size stays the same. The distance manipulation separated intensity from the real cube size in each trial, so a fixed intensity criterion could not match the reward across every combination of distances. The rewarded size was the stable reference across trials.

Image diameter behaved in the same way, and its measured width grew with each increase in distance, so the image changed while the reward did not. Width fails as a stand-in for size, and the fish's choices followed the physical cube instead of the image it produced. Image intensity and image width were the two candidate cues for size.

Darkness controls showed that the size discrimination survived without visual input, which suggests an electrosensory route for the learned choice. Cubes were moved to new distances in separate tests, while each cube's rewarded size stayed fixed across them. The learned preference still held when each cube's distance changed relative to the gates.
notes: Image intensity and diameter both shift with distance.

A rule based on image intensity fails here because intensity falls as an object moves away, while the rewarded physical size stays the same

The distance manipulation separated intensity from the real cube size in each trial, so a fixed intensity criterion could not match the reward across every combination of distances. The rewarded size was the stable reference across trials.

inserts.title: Discharge timing shapes each approach sample
paragraphs: Spatial sampling density is the number of electric discharges per distance traveled. It depends jointly on emission timing and swimming speed, so a fish that swims faster collects fewer discharges per centimeter unless it also raises its discharge rate. Density reflects two behaviors at once, the emission pattern and the movement. This ratio is the quantity that changes during each approach.

Each electric sample reaches the skin while the object's image is changing, so each discharge carries a different spatial context. Hofmann and colleagues paired the discharge record with the approach trajectory, which let each sample be matched to the fish's position at that moment. The recorded discharge timing supplied the sampling record for every approach.

Thrust and discharge activity moved in opposite directions across the approach, and the sampling density rose as the fish closed in. Straighter postures and more direct alignment with the object accompanied that rise in density, so the geometry of inspection and the sample sequence changed together. The approach geometry was measured as well as the electric samples.
notes: Discharge timing shapes each approach sample.

inserts.title: Normalization removes the amplitude scale
paragraphs: A relative gradient divides the rate of amplitude change by the current amplitude, so its output depends on the shape of the change rather than on absolute size. For that reason the relative-gradient curves overlapped across cube sizes that produced very different absolute amplitudes, which is the central result of this comparison. The ratio thus discounts the overall scale of the signal.

Adapted emission and movement produced more samples near each cube than unadapted patterns did, so the cue depends on the animal's own sampling pattern in every trial. Adapted emission changes how many measurements feed the gradient at each distance, and that change is built into the reconstruction. Each cube size yielded its own sampling profile.

The gradient cue was built from reconstructed frames and tested inside the modeled input. The reconstruction supplies the candidate signal, while the neurons that would use that signal were not part of the model. Relative gradients give the same distance information across the cube sizes tested. The absolute amplitude, by contrast, carries size information that tracks object size rather than distance.
notes: Normalization removes the amplitude scale.

inserts.title: Dynamic cues reach threshold farther away
paragraphs: The detection criterion defines when an object's information first rises above the variability of the reference condition. Under that criterion, the dynamic cue crossed threshold at about 6 cm, while the static image measure crossed it at about 3 cm, so the dynamic cue carried information to a greater distance. The paper defined that criterion for the reconstructed cues.

The dynamic measure also resolved distance more finely at longer distances in the modeled data. That resolution describes what the reconstructed cue can separate, which is an analysis result rather than a value recorded from the fish, and it is computed from the same reconstructed approaches. Both cues were judged over the same range of simulated distances.

The roughly 4 cm recognition range in the choice tasks is a separate measure of identification. Shape discrimination and distance estimation require different kinds of information, so the two thresholds can differ in value even when both come from the same object. The two ranges were measured in different experiments, so the two numbers answer different questions.
notes: Dynamic cues reach threshold farther away.

inserts.title: Electrolocation alone reached high accuracy
paragraphs: Each group was defined by the senses it could use during testing, and each group was tested under its own condition. Every group reached at least 84% correct, so electrolocation by itself supported a high level of discrimination in this near-field task. Accuracy stayed at or above 84% in each group despite the different sensory inputs.

The gain from combining the senses was measured with the objects placed close to the gates, at about 1 cm, where electric information is strongest for these fish. Both sensory channels were available together in the combined condition, so the difference reflects the information each channel supplied. The electric route alone supported accurate choices at close range.

The rewarded-object choice stayed identical across those conditions, so accuracy differences reflect the sensory information available to each group. Final accuracy and the number of training days are separate outcomes, one describing the stable endpoint and the other the speed of learning. Placement at the gates was identical across the three groups and in every test session.
notes: Electrolocation alone reached high accuracy.

inserts.title: Latency adds timing to amplitude information
paragraphs: The first spike of a mormyromast afferent appears at a latency measured from the electric stimulus. A larger amplitude shortens that latency, so the spike's timing carries amplitude information that a spike count alone lacks. The latency is measured from stimulus onset, so it reflects the timing of a single neuron's response. Each recording reflects one afferent's timing.

The brief pulses were chosen to resemble an EOD, which allowed amplitude to vary while the sampling interval was held apart from it. Each recorded response was tied to a controlled pulse, and its latency could be read directly from the recording. The pulses were controlled, so the same stimulus could be repeated for each amplitude and interval.

Timing information is available within a single spike, before the count of a whole burst is known. The latency code is one way the afferent represents local electric contrast, and it operates at the level of a single fiber rather than a population. Latency adds a second dimension to the afferent response, beyond how many spikes were fired.
notes: Latency adds timing to amplitude information.

inserts.title: Natural interval sequences change latency
paragraphs: The replay used natural EOD interval sequences, so each pulse in the sequence carried its own preceding interval. Latency changed from pulse to pulse as those intervals varied, a pattern that a fixed-rate stimulus lacks entirely. The replay kept the sequence of natural pulses intact across each trial. Fixed-rate pulses lack the variability of that sequence.

Amplitude modulation was delivered as a controlled comparison input, so the replayed intervals and the amplitude changes were recorded in the same afferents. This arrangement isolated how the interval sequence shifted the response while the amplitude input was held constant. The amplitude input was constant across the replayed intervals, which isolated the interval effect. Latency was read on every replayed pulse.

The same local amplitude gave a different latency depending on the sequence that preceded it, which places sampling history inside the afferent code. The afferent carries information about the timing of active sampling itself, alongside the electric contrast. Sampling history is a property of the animal's own sensing, since the animal generates the intervals. Every sequence was run through the same afferents.
notes: Natural interval sequences change latency.

inserts.title: Interval-dependent gain improves latency fits
paragraphs: Interval-dependent sensitivity was added as a term that changes the amplitude gain according to previous intervals. The model with this term predicted measured latencies better than a model that ignored interval history, which is the main result of the fitting exercise. The added term changes gain with the previous intervals, not with the present amplitude alone.

The fit used the same recorded afferent responses, so the improvement came from representing stimulus history rather than from new data. Prediction failures were most visible when natural intervals were combined with slowly correlated amplitudes, which is the condition the model had to reproduce. Prediction failures were examined separately for each interval pattern. The fits were checked against the recorded latencies.

The fitted model names the variables that govern the history dependence of the latency code. A model of this kind can make predictions for responses to interval sequences that were not part of the original fit, so it extends beyond the recorded examples. Such models summarize the afferent's input-output relation in a form that can be tested on new sequences.
notes: Interval-dependent gain improves latency fits.

inserts.title: Excitation in the ELL uses two glutamate receptors
paragraphs: Glutamate-gated ion channels of the AMPA and NMDA types carry the excitatory current evoked by parallel-fiber input. Their pharmacology was examined separately in the same slice preparation, so each receptor type could be tested on its own. Their contributions were separated by drug application. The NMDA and AMPA receptors are distinguished by their antagonists, which were applied in separate tests.

Removing magnesium increased the NMDA component of the response, which shows that magnesium blocks the NMDA channel at normal resting voltage. Washing out the antagonists restored the response, so the drug effect was reversible rather than a sign of tissue damage. The reversibility argument rests on recovery after washout in the same tissue. Recovery confirmed the reversibility of that effect.

The two receptor types respond to the same transmitter, so their relative contributions depend on the state of the postsynaptic membrane at the moment of input. The slice results name the receptor types that contribute in this preparation. The field response combines these contributions and gives no count of receptors per synapse. Their pharmacology identifies the contributing receptors.
notes: Excitation in the ELL uses two glutamate receptors.

inserts.title: Facilitation depends on the spacing of two pulses
paragraphs: Paired-pulse facilitation was measured as the ratio of the second EPSP to the first, using pulse pairs spaced across tens to hundreds of milliseconds. Facilitation was strongest at the shortest spacings tested, which means the effect fades as the gap between pulses lengthens. Facilitation was tested across that whole range. Pulse spacing was the variable that changed across the pairs.

Independent stimulation sites separated repeated stimulation of one fiber population from activation of a different population. Each site produced its own pair of responses, which made the source of facilitation identifiable in the recordings. Facilitation depends on which fibers are recruited as well as on the interval. The two cases differ in which fibers respond to the second pulse.

Short-term facilitation enlarges the response of a synapse that was used moments earlier, so the next input has a larger effect on the cell. Long-lasting changes need repeated spike pairings, a separate process from the short-term change measured in these recordings. Its time course follows the spacing of the paired stimuli, which is why the interval is the key variable.
notes: Facilitation depends on the spacing of two pulses.

inserts.title: Efferent cells respond to both input layers
paragraphs: Output neurons of two kinds, large ganglion cells and fusiform cells, were recorded in these slices alongside the medium ganglion interneurons. Their firing to current injection was set against that of the interneurons, which provides a second cell type for comparison. Their current-evoked firing was recorded for each cell type. Those recordings sampled cells of different types within one slice.

Excitatory and inhibitory influences reached these output cells, and the balance between them depended on the stimulated pathway. A fusiform cell has an elongated cell body, which distinguishes its morphology from that of the Purkinje-like interneuron in the same structure. The balance was tested for each pathway and cell in these recordings. The stimulated pathway determined which influence dominated.

The output cells form a separate route out of the ELL, while the medium ganglion interneuron contributes to the local circuit. Local responses are one stage of the processing that precedes the output neurons in each slice. Circuit position determines whether a local signal reaches the output neurons. Behavior-level interpretation requires intact animal experiments.
notes: Efferent cells respond to both input layers.

inserts.title: B spikes and N spikes are separate events
paragraphs: Broad dendritic events, called B spikes, are tied to plasticity at parallel-fiber synapses. Both event classes arise in one medium ganglion cell, which allows their timing to be compared directly within a single recording. Their timing relative to the command can be compared on a shared reference. Both event classes were examined in each recording.

B-spike timing shifted across the phases of the electric-organ command cycle, and specific N-spike patterns were found near each B spike. These associations were made within the same cell during the same recording sessions, so the two event types were observed together. Their relative timing was tracked across cycles. Their relation to the command cycle was examined phase by phase.

Keeping the two event types apart matters because they reach different targets within one cell. A broad spike regulates later synaptic change, while a narrow spike carries the cell's immediate signal outward to the rest of the circuit. The narrow spike carries the immediate output, and the broad spike feeds back on synaptic strength. Both events remain distinguishable in the same recording.
notes: B spikes and N spikes are separate events.

inserts.title: A transient rise follows stimulus removal
paragraphs: The recordings captured the state that the circuit entered during repeated electrosensory stimulation, and they tracked that state into the command cycles that followed. Switching the stimulus off produced a transient increase in early B-spike activity. The recordings examined the cycles that followed each stimulation episode. Command-linked recordings were analyzed in the cycles immediately after stimulation ended.

That rise appeared although the command signal served as the timing reference throughout. Stimulus history shaped when and how often these events occurred, not merely whether they occurred in a given cycle. Switching off the stimulus changed the timing of B spikes within the early cycles. This change in early timing is what the transient increase consists of.

The transient response is a candidate learned prediction, and additional inhibition and pairing experiments are needed to identify the mechanism behind it. The observed firing pattern is the measured result, while the mechanism is an interpretation of that result. The circuit state built during stimulation provides one explanation for the rise. Each candidate mechanism predicts a different time course for the transient.
notes: A transient rise follows stimulus removal.

2: Active electrolocation is the detection of nearby objects through changes in an electric field that the animal generates itself. The weakly electric elephantnose fish, Gnathonemus petersii, emits brief **electric organ discharges**, or EODs, and senses how surrounding objects alter the current flowing across its skin. Each discharge therefore samples the nearby objects again.

Von der Emde and colleagues trained fish to choose between three-dimensional objects in a two-alternative task, with each trial offering a pair of objects. Recognition persisted in complete darkness, including tests of object size and rotation, so visible appearance was not needed under those conditions. Accurate choices in the dark therefore point to a nonvisual capacity.

This behavior concerns near-field sensing rather than a long-range image of the environment. In the tested tasks, object recognition failed beyond about 4 cm, even though the electric field itself extends farther from the fish. Recognition at that range therefore depends on the fish's own electric field, which carries the object's effect to the skin.
3: An **electric image** is the spatial pattern of object-induced change in current across the fish's skin. An object whose conductivity differs from the water around it changes the local electric field, so the pattern carries information about that object. The sensory skin registers that pattern across many locations at once, and each location contributes a different part of it.

Hofmann and colleagues recorded spontaneous approaches to metal cubes and reconstructed electric images with a biophysical model. Comparing object-present and object-absent simulations isolated the perturbation that the object produced along the sensory surface. The model used measured behavior as its constraint, so each estimate reflects the movements the fish actually made during each approach.

The reconstructed images changed over successive discharges as the fish approached the object. These are model-based estimates rather than direct recordings from every receptor, so each frame is a predicted current pattern that approximates the object's geometry closely. The sequence of frames therefore follows the fish's approach from distance to close inspection.
4: **Generalization** is preservation of a learned response when conditions differ from training. Von der Emde and colleagues trained an elephantnose fish to recognize a compound object, a cone with a sphere above it, while varying the alternative object across trials. The alternative changed from one trial to the next, so no single pair was ever repeated.

After about three months of training, the fish preferred the rewarded object over both familiar alternatives and two previously unfamiliar objects. Test trials carried no reward or punishment, so the new pairings were never reinforced during testing. Each familiar alternative was an object the fish had already seen during training, and preference was measured across all of the pairs.

Recognition therefore depended on features shared by the positive object rather than on memorizing one fixed pair. The fish's preference extended to objects it had never been trained against, which makes generalization the defining feature of this task. Electrical and movement-dependent cues could both supply the features that guided the choice in each trial.
5: A **component cue** is an identifiable part of a larger object that can contribute to recognition. The compound training object had a sphere, a cone, and a narrow junction, so von der Emde and colleagues could test each part as a separate stimulus against novel alternatives. The intact object served as the reference for every component test.

The sphere kept much of the preference that the intact object produced. The cone gave lower choice frequencies, roughly 70% or 59% depending on the alternative, and a stimulus mimicking the narrow junction also reduced recognition. Each component therefore produced its own level of recognition, measured against the same novel alternatives that the intact object faced.

The parts were therefore not equally effective, so learned object features are used selectively. Choices reveal this selectivity at the level of behavior, and removing one component changes the electric pattern available to the animal. Recognition of the compound object rests on several learned components rather than on any one of them alone.

Sawtell and colleagues examined command-evoked membrane responses at different holding potentials, using their voltage dependence to separate excitatory and inhibitory contributions in ELL cells. The voltage dependence sorted the currents by reversal behavior in each cell.

Recordings showed inhibition during command-evoked excitation, including in medium ganglion cells. A reduced B-spike probability therefore coexists with excitatory drive in that interval. Inhibition was present during the excitatory phase of the command response. Changes across holding potentials helped separate the two synaptic currents. The response differed between the excitatory and inhibitory phases.

Concurrent inputs affect dendritic firing and axonal output differently because their timing, location, and reversal properties differ. Conductance analysis constrains those contributions to the intact command response. Holding potential changes the driving force for each synaptic current. Each conductance was read from the voltage dependence of the response. Those readings constrain the input balance.
44: **Disinhibition** is increased activity following removal of an inhibitory influence. Sawtell and colleagues injected bicuculline locally into the ventral molecular layer, blocking GABA-A receptor-mediated inhibition while recording command-linked medium ganglion spikes. The local antagonist was applied at a defined depth in the molecular layer. The effect was measured against the baseline command response.

B-spike also probability rose strongly just after the injection, with much less immediate change in N-spike output. Superficial injections had weaker effects on B spikes, which gives a spatial contrast across injection sites. Superficial and deeper injections were tested separately. Injection depth was the variable that set the size of the change.

This manipulation supports strong inhibitory control over dendritic events. The injection acts on a local network rather than one identified synapse, so the selectivity holds for the tested timing and locations. Local antagonist application provides causal evidence that the blocked receptor contributes to suppression. The deeper and more superficial injections constrain where the inhibitory influence is expressed.
45: **Spike-timing-dependent plasticity** is a lasting synaptic change whose direction depends on the relative timing of activity. Sawtell and colleagues repeatedly evoked a B spike at defined delays, approximately 8-110 ms after the electric-organ command, then measured command-evoked responses before and after pairing. The pairing delays ranged from about 8 to 110 ms after the command.

Pairing near the peak of the command response tended to reduce later excitation, whereas earlier or later pairings could enhance it. The changes in N-spike output tied the altered synaptic response to the cell's principal output event. The pairing delays set the timing relative to the command peak, which determined the direction of the change.

Timing-dependent also adaptation is established in this studied circuit. Command context, dendritic events, synaptic strength, and axonal activity are connected, so the adaptation links learning-related signals to the cell's output. A change in output after pairing supports a functional consequence of synaptic adaptation. The behavioral readout is a separate level of evidence.
